title: Low-Rank Approximation
body:
Keep the first $k$ terms of the [[Singular Value Decomposition]] and throw the rest away:

$$
A_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\,\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^T
$$

$A_k$ has rank $k$ by construction. The **Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem** says it is the best such
matrix there is:

$$
\|A - A_k\|_F \leq \|A - B\|_F \quad \text{for every } B \text{ of rank} \leq k
$$

and the same holds in the spectral norm. **No other rank-$k$ matrix is closer to $A$**, in either
norm, and the error is exactly the tail you discarded:

$$
\|A - A_k\|_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2}, \qquad \|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}
$$

That is an unusually strong statement for an approximation method. Most of them are heuristics you
justify afterwards; this one is provably optimal, and the proof is one line of
[[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormality]] once you have the sum-of-rank-ones form.

## Why it compresses

An $m \times n$ matrix costs $mn$ numbers. $A_k$ costs $k(m + n + 1)$: $k$ singular values plus
$k$ vectors of each length. For a $1000 \times 1000$ image and $k = 50$ that is 100,050 numbers
against a million, a **10x** saving, and the error is whatever $\sigma_{51}$ onwards adds up to.

The saving is only real when the singular values decay fast, and the useful fact is that **real
data almost always does**. Columns of a dataset are correlated, pixels of an image resemble their
neighbours, and users rate films in patterns. Correlation means near-dependence, near-dependence
means small singular values, and small singular values mean the matrix was nearly rank $k$ to
begin with. Plotting $\sigma_i$ on a log scale and looking for the elbow is the standard way to
pick $k$, the same plot [[Principal Component Analysis]] calls a scree plot.

## Where it turns up

- **[[Image Processing]]**: the compression demo of the course, and the one you can see.
- **[[Principal Component Analysis]]**: PCA is this theorem applied to a centred data matrix, so
  "keep the top $k$ components" is "keep the top $k$ singular values" and inherits the optimality
  proof. That inheritance is why PCA can claim to lose the least possible variance rather than
  merely a small amount.
- **Latent semantic analysis and recommender systems**: factor a documents-by-terms or
  users-by-items matrix into $k$ hidden factors, and entries that were missing get predicted by
  the low-rank reconstruction.
- **Denoising**: signal is usually low rank and structured, noise is full rank and spread across
  every $\sigma_i$. Truncating removes proportionally more noise than signal.
- **Model compression**: replacing a neural network's weight matrix with a rank-$k$ factorisation
  cuts both parameters and multiply-adds in the [[Forward Pass]].
